diagrams.title: The CIA Triad: Three Pillars, One Asset
diagrams.subtitle: Click a pillar then its control: confidentiality, integrity, and availability together protect data.

nodes.label: Confidentiality
nodes.detail: Only authorized parties access the data: encryption, MFA, ACLs, and segmentation.
nodes.exam: CIA: C = confidentiality, not 'control'.

nodes.label: Integrity
nodes.detail: Data is not modified without authorization: hashing, digital signatures, version control.
nodes.exam: A hash detects modification; a signature also proves origin.

nodes.label: Availability
nodes.detail: Reliable, continuous access: redundancy, backups, SLAs, and DDoS protection.
nodes.exam: Ransomware primarily attacks availability and confidentiality.

nodes.label: Controls
nodes.detail: Preventive controls restrict reading: encryption at rest/in transit, MFA, access control lists.
nodes.exam: Classify data before choosing the control.

nodes.label: Controls
nodes.detail: Hashes, signatures, logging, and access control ensure integrity.
nodes.exam: A hash alone does not prove origin: add a signature.

nodes.label: Controls
nodes.detail: Clustering, tested backups, redundant power, and monitoring maintain service.
nodes.exam: An untested backup is not proof of availability.

nodes.label: Protected Asset
nodes.detail: All three pillars apply to an identified asset: data, system, or identity.
nodes.exam: Always start by identifying and classifying the asset.

nodes.label: CIA Trade-off
nodes.detail: Balance depends on context: a military system prioritizes confidentiality, a bank prioritizes integrity.
nodes.exam: The exam tests CIA trade-offs in real-world scenarios.

quiz.question: Which pillar ensures that data has not been modified without authorization?

diagrams.title: The AAA Flow: Identity, Proof, Rights, Logs
diagrams.subtitle: Follow the access chain: authentication precedes authorization, and accounting makes the action auditable.

nodes.label: Identity
nodes.detail: Establish who is requesting access: user account, service account, certificate, or federated identity.
nodes.exam: Identity is declared before any proof.

nodes.label: Authentication
nodes.detail: Verify identity with a knowledge factor (password), possession factor (token), or inherence factor (biometrics).
nodes.exam: MFA = two factors from different categories.

nodes.label: Authorization
nodes.detail: Determine rights after authentication: RBAC, ABAC, least privilege, and approval.
nodes.exam: Authorization always comes after authentication.

nodes.label: Accounting
nodes.detail: Record who did what, when, and from where: logs, timestamps, SIEM.
nodes.exam: Accounting = traceability, not financial accounting.

nodes.label: Audit
nodes.detail: Use logs to detect abuse and reconstruct an incident.
nodes.exam: Without NTP, log correlation is impossible.

nodes.label: Policy
nodes.detail: Policy defines the access rules enforced by technical controls.
nodes.exam: Rule precedes tool: policy before technology.

nodes.label: MFA
nodes.detail: Add a second factor to resist password theft and phishing.
nodes.exam: A FIDO2 key is stronger than an SMS code.

nodes.label: Monitoring
nodes.detail: Monitor deviations: alerts, UEBA, and periodic access reviews.
nodes.exam: Access reviews detect privilege creep.

quiz.question: Which AAA step records who did what and when?

diagrams.title: Controls Grid: Category × Type
diagrams.subtitle: Click a cell: the row gives the control type, and the column gives the control category.

cells.detail: Prevents the action before it happens: security policies, awareness training, separation of duties.
Blocks or renders unauthorized access unreadable: classic preventive technical controls.
Physically prevents access to sensitive areas: physical access control.
Discovers anomalies after the fact through audit records and periodic reviews.
Detects attack signals and correlates events in real time.
Signals a physical intrusion and provides video evidence.
Organizes remediation: incident response, communication, lessons learned.
Fixes or cleans up after an incident: patching, quarantine, backup restoration.
Limits and remediates physical damage after an event.
Compensates for the inability to apply a standard control with an approved equivalent measure.
Isolates an unprotectable resource to reduce the impact of exploitation.
Replaces an absent access control with temporary human supervision.

diagrams.title: Change Window: From Ticket to Closure
diagrams.subtitle: A change window is time-boxed: request, CAB, preparation, freeze, execution, and verification.

nodes.label: RFC Request
nodes.detail: Document scope, risks, rollback plan, and success criteria.
nodes.exam: A change without a rollback plan is rejected by the CAB.

nodes.label: CAB
nodes.detail: The Change Advisory Board approves, defers, or rejects the request after impact analysis.
nodes.exam: The CAB brings together IT, security, and business stakeholders.

nodes.label: Planning
nodes.detail: Define steps, dependencies, resources, tests, and success criteria.
nodes.exam: Set success criteria before execution.

nodes.label: Communication
nodes.detail: Inform users and teams of the window and expected disruptions.
nodes.exam: Good communication reduces perceived impact.

nodes.label: Freeze
nodes.detail: Suspend other changes to avoid collisions during the window.
nodes.exam: A change freeze is often applied at fiscal year-end.

nodes.label: Execution
nodes.detail: Apply the change with a prior backup and continuous monitoring.
nodes.exam: Exceeding the window requires requesting an extension.

nodes.label: Verification
nodes.detail: Check functional tests, logs, and success criteria.
nodes.exam: Verification always precedes closure.

nodes.label: Closure
nodes.detail: Close the ticket, update documentation, and update the CMDB inventory.
nodes.exam: The CMDB must reflect the actual state after the change.

quiz.question: Who approves or rejects a change request in committee?

diagrams.title: Failed Rollback: The Domino Effect
diagrams.subtitle: A poorly prepared rollback can cause more damage than the initial change.

nodes.label: Change
nodes.detail: The change is deployed and initial checks fail.
nodes.exam: Early detection limits the scope of the rollback.

nodes.label: Anomaly
nodes.detail: An application error or service outage appears during the window.
nodes.exam: Define a decision threshold before starting.

nodes.label: Decision
nodes.detail: The owner decides to revert, ideally within the original window.
nodes.exam: A late rollback increases the risk of data loss.

nodes.label: Restoration
nodes.detail: The previous configuration or pre-change backup is restored.
nodes.exam: Test restoration before the change, not during.

nodes.label: Inconsistent State
nodes.detail: The restored version no longer matches current data or dependencies.
nodes.exam: The delta between two versions is the classic trap.

nodes.label: Data Loss
nodes.detail: Data created after the change is lost or corrupted by the restoration.
nodes.exam: A restore overwrites recent writes.

nodes.label: Outage
nodes.detail: The service remains unavailable: the impact exceeds that of the initial change.
nodes.exam: A failed rollback turns a minor incident into a major one.

nodes.label: Post-mortem
nodes.detail: Identify root cause, revise the rollback plan, and communicate.
nodes.exam: Lessons learned feed into the next CAB.

quiz.question: Which step causes the loss of recent writes?

diagrams.title: From Password to Hash: Salt and Slow KDF
diagrams.subtitle: Passwords are never stored in plaintext: they are salted, hashed with a slow KDF, and then verified.

nodes.label: Password
nodes.detail: The password is a secret entered by the user; it must never be stored in plaintext.
nodes.exam: Plaintext storage = critical confidentiality failure.

nodes.label: Random Salt
nodes.detail: A unique random value generated per account and stored alongside the hash.
nodes.exam: The salt is not secret: it defeats rainbow tables.

nodes.label: Combination
nodes.detail: The secret and salt are concatenated before applying the key derivation function.
nodes.exam: The salt must be unique per user, not global.

nodes.label: Slow KDF
nodes.detail: A function with CPU/memory cost produces the hash: bcrypt, Argon2, or PBKDF2.
nodes.exam: Do not use a fast hash like SHA-256 for passwords.

nodes.label: Stored Hash
nodes.detail: The hash, salt, and cost parameters are saved in the identity database.
nodes.exam: Salt and parameters are required for verification.

nodes.label: Verification
nodes.detail: At login, the hash is recomputed using the stored salt and then compared.
nodes.exam: Comparison must be constant-time.

nodes.label: Computation Cost
nodes.detail: Iterations and memory slow down offline attacks on stolen hashes.
nodes.exam: Argon2 resists GPUs/ASICs better due to its memory cost.

nodes.label: Offline Attack
nodes.detail: Without a unique salt, rainbow tables and wordlists speed up cracking.
nodes.exam: A unique salt makes two identical passwords produce different hashes.

quiz.question: Which non-secret element prevents rainbow table attacks?

diagrams.title: Certificate Chain: Root, Leaf, Revocation
diagrams.subtitle: The client validates a trust chain up to a root, then checks that the leaf is not revoked.

nodes.label: Root CA
nodes.detail: Self-signed root authority kept offline: the trust anchor of the PKI.
nodes.exam: Compromising the root invalidates the entire chain.

nodes.label: Intermediate CA
nodes.detail: Intermediate authority that signs leaf certificates and limits exposure of the root.
nodes.exam: A short chain is simpler to validate.

nodes.label: Leaf Certificate
nodes.detail: Server certificate: name (SAN), public key, validity dates, and usage.
nodes.exam: Check the SAN, not just the CN.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.detail: The client checks the chain, hostname, expiration date, and revocation status.
nodes.exam: An expired certificate is rejected even if the chain is valid.

nodes.label: Trust Store
nodes.detail: Trust store containing the root authorities accepted by the system.
nodes.exam: Adding an arbitrary root destroys trust.

nodes.label: Revocation
nodes.detail: Verify that the certificate has not been canceled before its expiration date.
nodes.exam: CRL = downloaded list; OCSP = online query.

nodes.label: OCSP Stapling
nodes.detail: The server itself provides a recent, signed OCSP response.
nodes.exam: Stapling reduces load on the OCSP server.

nodes.label: Pinning
nodes.detail: The application accepts only a pre-expected key or authority.
nodes.exam: Pinning protects against a compromised CA but complicates renewal.

quiz.question: Which mechanism checks online that a certificate has not been canceled?

diagrams.title: Encryption Levels: From Disk to Field
diagrams.subtitle: Vertical stack of layers where encryption is applied, with one common requirement: key management.

nodes.label: Disk / FDE
nodes.detail: Full disk encryption: protects data at rest if the physical media is stolen.
nodes.exam: FDE does not protect against an already authenticated user.

nodes.label: Partition
nodes.detail: An encrypted partition isolates a logical space with its own key.
nodes.exam: Prefer FDE over partially encrypted partitions that may be forgotten.

nodes.label: Volume
nodes.detail: Volume encryption operates below the file system (LUKS, BitLocker).
nodes.exam: Volume = block layer; file = user layer.

nodes.label: File / EFS
nodes.detail: EFS encrypts files per user, offering fine-grained control but greater complexity.
nodes.exam: File encryption protects against other local accounts.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.detail: TDE encrypts the database at rest; column encryption protects sensitive fields.
nodes.exam: TDE is transparent: the application does not change.

nodes.label: Record
nodes.detail: Record-level encryption protects each field (PII, secrets).
nodes.exam: The finer the granularity, the more complex key management becomes.

nodes.label: Key Management
nodes.detail: Keys protected by KMS/HSM with rotation and separation of duties.
nodes.exam: Without key management, encryption provides no real protection.

quiz.question: Which layer encrypts an individual field such as a card number?

diagrams.title: Threat Intelligence Cycle
diagrams.subtitle: A continuous cycle: plan, collect, analyze, disseminate, and evaluate, with storage and prioritization.

nodes.label: Plan
nodes.detail: Define requirements (PIR), critical assets, and the questions to answer.
nodes.exam: The cycle starts with a question, not blind collection.

nodes.label: Collect
nodes.detail: Collect internal logs, OSINT, threat feeds, and human intelligence.
nodes.exam: Evaluate the relevance and reliability of each source.

nodes.label: Analyze
nodes.detail: Correlate indicators, reconstruct TTPs, and characterize the threat.
nodes.exam: MITRE ATT&CK structures tactic analysis.

nodes.label: Disseminate
nodes.detail: Deliver as a brief, report, or structured STIX/TAXII feed.
nodes.exam: The right recipient gets the right level of detail.

nodes.label: Evaluate
nodes.detail: Measure the usefulness of the intelligence and close gaps in the cycle.
nodes.exam: Feedback is mandatory to close the loop.

nodes.label: Store
nodes.detail: Retain IOCs and reports with timestamps, provenance, and confidence level.
nodes.exam: Without provenance, an indicator loses its value.

nodes.label: Prioritize
nodes.detail: Weight intelligence by confidence, relevance, and business urgency.
nodes.exam: Not all threats deserve the same attention.

quiz.question: Which step reconstructs an adversary's tactics and techniques?

diagrams.title: CVSS: Severity × Exposure
diagrams.subtitle: Click a cell: the CVSS score gives severity, while exposure and context determine priority.

cells.detail: Low severity, often limited impact. Track the flaw without emergency mobilization.
Even a low score becomes concerning on the Internet or when chained with other flaws.
Moderate severity: include the patch in the next change window.
Public exposure increases the likelihood of automated exploitation.
Serious impact: schedule a priority patch and enhanced monitoring.
Internet exposure + known exploit = very short window before exploitation.
Prepare patch, isolation, or compensating control; notify stakeholders.
Emergency patch or take the service offline: the risk is critical and exploitable.

diagrams.title: Threat Actors and Motivations
diagrams.subtitle: Link each actor to its motivation, then to the attributes useful for analysis.

nodes.label: APT / Nation-State
nodes.detail: State-sponsored group, patient and highly targeted, often active for years.
nodes.exam: APT = Advanced Persistent Threat: specific target and long duration.

nodes.label: Cybercriminal
nodes.detail: Profit-driven actor: fraud, ransomware, data theft and resale.
nodes.exam: Cybercriminals seek return on investment.

nodes.label: Hacktivist
nodes.detail: Actor driven by a political or social cause: defacement, leaks, DDoS.
nodes.exam: Hacktivism ≠ espionage: visibility comes first.

nodes.label: Insider
nodes.detail: Authorized person who abuses access out of revenge, money, or coercion.
nodes.exam: Insiders are often detected by UEBA, not by the firewall.

nodes.label: Data Theft
nodes.detail: Objective: steal secrets, intellectual property, or strategic information.
nodes.exam: Espionage primarily targets confidentiality.

nodes.label: Extortion
nodes.detail: Encryption or exfiltration for ransom, with double extortion.
nodes.exam: Double extortion = encryption + threat of publication.

nodes.label: Disruption
nodes.detail: Objective: disrupt service and broadcast a political message.
nodes.exam: A DDoS targets availability.

nodes.label: Attributes
nodes.detail: Attribution clues: TTPs, infrastructure, languages, time zones, and targets.
nodes.exam: Attributes help correlate, never prove on their own.

quiz.question: Which actor acts primarily for an ideological or political cause?

diagrams.title: Attribution: From Association to Certainty
diagrams.subtitle: Correlating indicators is not proof: certainty requires multiple independent sources.

nodes.label: Technical Traces
nodes.detail: Initial collected indicators: IP addresses, file hashes, domains, and logs.
nodes.exam: An isolated IOC proves nothing.

nodes.label: Association
nodes.detail: Link similar indicators to a previously known campaign or group.
nodes.exam: Association ≠ attribution.

nodes.label: Infrastructure
nodes.detail: Infrastructure reuse: command servers, certificates, hosting.
nodes.exam: Infrastructure can be shared or rented.

nodes.label: TTPs
nodes.detail: Tactics, techniques, and procedures are more durable than simple indicators.
nodes.exam: Compare modus operandi, not just hashes.

nodes.label: Confidence Level
nodes.detail: Express a degree of confidence based on the quality and independence of sources.
nodes.exam: A report must explicitly state uncertainty.

nodes.label: Certain Attribution
nodes.detail: Attribution accepted when multiple independent sources agree.
nodes.exam: Public attribution is political as well as technical.

nodes.label: False Flag
nodes.detail: An adversary may plant false indicators to steer the investigation toward another actor.
nodes.exam: Never conclude based on a single indicator.

nodes.label: Communication
nodes.detail: Deliver the finding as a report and share it with peers.
nodes.exam: Sharing strengthens collective defense.

quiz.question: Which concept rates the reliability of an attribution before publishing it?

diagrams.title: Attack Vector Families
diagrams.subtitle: Vectors are entry points: click a family to see how it operates.

nodes.label: Message
nodes.detail: Phishing, spear-phishing, SMiShing, or vishing: the message carries the lure.
nodes.exam: Spear-phishing = targeted; whaling = executives.

nodes.label: Image / File
nodes.detail: Images, documents, and attachments can hide code or metadata.
nodes.exam: An image can contain a payload (polyglot).

nodes.label: Network
nodes.detail: Interception, DNS poisoning, weak protocols, and exposed services.
nodes.exam: The network vector exploits trust between machines.

nodes.label: Endpoint
nodes.detail: USB drives, vulnerable browsers, Office macros, and local applications.
nodes.exam: Macros remain a classic exam vector.

nodes.label: Entry Point
nodes.detail: A vector becomes an intrusion path only if it meets an exploitable weakness.
nodes.exam: Vector alone ≠ incident: a vulnerability is needed.

nodes.label: Supply Chain
nodes.detail: Compromised dependencies, signed updates, and trusted third parties.
nodes.exam: SolarWinds illustrates a signed-update supply chain attack.

nodes.label: Cloud / Identity
nodes.detail: Misconfigured OAuth, stolen tokens, exposed APIs, and public buckets.
nodes.exam: A cloud misconfiguration is a vector, not a code flaw.

nodes.label: Human Signals
nodes.detail: Social engineering: pretexting, phone calls, messages, and public information.
nodes.exam: The human vector bypasses technical controls.

quiz.question: Which family covers attacks delivered through a compromised software update?

diagrams.title: Supply Chain Attack: From Vendor to Client
diagrams.subtitle: Malicious code is introduced upstream and distributed through a channel the client trusts.

nodes.label: Vendor
nodes.detail: The software publisher or vendor is the trusted source attacked upstream.
nodes.exam: A trusted third party expands the attack surface.

nodes.label: Build Pipeline
nodes.detail: The integration pipeline or repository is compromised: malicious code is injected.
nodes.exam: Protect with commit signing, MFA, and code review.

nodes.label: Update
nodes.detail: The package is signed and distributed through the official distribution channel.
nodes.exam: A valid signature does not guarantee clean code.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.detail: The client installs the update without suspicion because the channel is expected.
nodes.exam: Trust in the channel is the exploit.

nodes.label: Implicit Trust
nodes.detail: The trust mechanism removes suspicion and accelerates deployment.
nodes.exam: Verify origin and integrity, not just the signature.

nodes.label: Compromise
nodes.detail: Malicious code runs with the privileges of the updated application.
nodes.exam: A single update compromises all clients at once.

nodes.label: Propagation
nodes.detail: Persistence and lateral movement extend impact beyond the initial host.
nodes.exam: Monitor for unusual outbound connections.

nodes.label: Detection
nodes.detail: SBOM, version diff analysis, EDR, and threat hunting reveal the anomaly.
nodes.exam: SBOM = inventory of software components.

quiz.question: Which step explains why the client accepts a malicious update without checking?

diagrams.title: System Attack Surface
diagrams.subtitle: Every entry point matters: network, code, credentials, configuration, and data.

nodes.label: Target System
nodes.detail: The attack surface encompasses all points through which an adversary can interact.
nodes.exam: Reducing the surface = disabling what is unnecessary.

nodes.label: Open Ports
nodes.detail: Each open port is a potential entry door discovered by scanning.
nodes.exam: A network scan starts with ports.

nodes.label: Services
nodes.detail: Exposed services, outdated versions, and banners that reveal technology.
nodes.exam: An unpatched service is a known vulnerability.

nodes.label: Application Code
nodes.detail: Applications, APIs, and forms: user inputs and business logic.
nodes.exam: All input is hostile (OWASP).

nodes.label: Credentials
nodes.detail: Accounts, tokens, and keys: weak, stolen, or over-privileged credentials.
nodes.exam: An over-privileged account increases impact.

nodes.label: Configuration
nodes.detail: Default settings, active debug mode, and overly broad access control lists.
nodes.exam: Misconfiguration = leading cause of cloud incidents.

nodes.label: Data / Shares
nodes.detail: Network shares, buckets, and exports accessible without proper control.
nodes.exam: Check permissions, not just existence.

nodes.label: Reduction
nodes.detail: Close ports, disable unnecessary services, and enforce least privilege.
nodes.exam: Hardening is a preventive control.

quiz.question: Which element groups accounts, tokens, and keys in the attack surface?

diagrams.title: Vulnerability Tree by Layer
diagrams.subtitle: Single root, five technical branches, one common impact: classify the weakness before scoring it.

nodes.label: Vulnerabilities
nodes.detail: Vulnerabilities are classified by technical layer to guide remediation.
nodes.exam: CWE classifies, CVE identifies, CVSS scores.

nodes.label: System / OS
nodes.detail: Kernel, system services, excessive privileges, and missing patches.
nodes.exam: An OS patch fixes the cause, not the symptom.

nodes.label: Network
nodes.detail: Exposed ports, unencrypted protocols, interception, and weak DNS.
nodes.exam: Sniffing exploits the lack of encryption.

nodes.label: Application
nodes.detail: SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, and unrestricted file uploads.
nodes.exam: The OWASP Top 10 is essential for the exam.

nodes.label: Code
nodes.detail: Memory overflow, deserialization, and hardcoded secrets.
nodes.exam: Hardcoded secrets are weakness CWE-798.

nodes.label: Cloud / Config
nodes.detail: Overly broad IAM, public bucket, SSRF via metadata, and exposed secrets.
nodes.exam: The shared responsibility model does not remove your obligations.

nodes.label: Impact
nodes.detail: A weakness becomes a concrete risk when a threat can exploit it.
nodes.exam: Exposure + public exploit = high priority.

quiz.question: Which branch covers a misconfigured public storage bucket?

diagrams.title: Malware Taxonomy
diagrams.subtitle: Virus, worm, Trojan, ransomware, rootkit, and fileless: distinguish propagation and stealth.

nodes.label: Malware
nodes.detail: Generic category: any software designed to harm, spread, or gain access.
nodes.exam: Malware is the generic term; the others are subtypes.

nodes.label: Virus
nodes.detail: Attaches to a file or sector and activates when the host is executed.
nodes.exam: A virus needs a host, unlike a worm.

nodes.label: Worm
nodes.detail: Spreads on its own across the network without user interaction or a host file.
nodes.exam: Worm = self-propagation, such as WannaCry.

nodes.label: Trojan
nodes.detail: Presents itself as legitimate software while hiding a malicious payload.
nodes.exam: A Trojan does not infect: it deceives the user.

nodes.label: Ransomware
nodes.detail: Encrypts files or exfiltrates data in exchange for a ransom payment.
nodes.exam: Offline backups and MFA are the best defenses.

nodes.label: Rootkit
nodes.detail: Hides processes, files, and connections, often at the kernel level.
nodes.exam: Detection: memory analysis and kernel integrity.

nodes.label: Fileless
nodes.detail: Lives in memory and abuses legitimate tools like PowerShell or WMI.
nodes.exam: Few disk IOCs: monitor behavior.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.detail: Search for hashes, network IOCs, behaviors, and memory footprints.
nodes.exam: TTPs are more durable than simple hashes.

quiz.question: Which malware spreads on its own without infecting a host file?

diagrams.title: Social Engineering: From Email to Compromise
diagrams.subtitle: The human vector bypasses technical controls: from deceptive link to session hijacking.

nodes.label: Email
nodes.detail: Spoofed message creating a sense of urgency with a link or attachment.
nodes.exam: Check the sender and domain, not just the body text.

nodes.label: Malicious Link
nodes.detail: Link to a counterfeit site or a lookalike domain (typosquatting).
nodes.exam: Hover over the link before clicking.

nodes.label: Credential Entry
nodes.detail: The victim enters their password into a counterfeit form.
nodes.exam: These forms also capture MFA codes.

nodes.label: MFA Bypass
nodes.detail: Adversary-in-the-middle attack or notification flooding to approve a login.
nodes.exam: FIDO2/WebAuthn resists phishing, unlike SMS.

nodes.label: Session Hijacking
nodes.detail: The session cookie is stolen and replayed to access the account.
nodes.exam: A stolen token makes the password irrelevant.

nodes.label: Compromise
nodes.detail: Access to the mailbox, financial fraud, and lateral movement.
nodes.exam: Revoke sessions and rotate tokens.

nodes.label: Reporting
nodes.detail: Report quickly to the SOC to limit the attacker's dwell time.
nodes.exam: Reporting drastically reduces impact.

nodes.label: Controls
nodes.detail: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, filters, training, and phishing-resistant authentication.
nodes.exam: Training is an administrative control.

quiz.question: Which mechanism allows stealing a session even when MFA is enabled?

diagrams.title: IOC Correlation: From Clues to Verdict
diagrams.subtitle: IP, hash, domain, and timestamp are enriched, correlated, and translated into a verdict and action.

nodes.label: IP Address
nodes.detail: Address of a command-and-control server or a scanner.
nodes.exam: A public IP can be shared: always corroborate.

nodes.label: SHA-256 Hash
nodes.detail: Fingerprint of a malicious file enabling precise detection.
nodes.exam: A hash changes if even a single byte changes.

nodes.label: Domain
nodes.detail: Algorithmically generated domain, phishing domain, or exfiltration domain.
nodes.exam: Correlate DNS, WHOIS, and query history.

nodes.label: Timestamp
nodes.detail: UTC timestamps of events enabling reconstruction of the causal chain.
nodes.exam: Synchronize clocks (NTP) before correlating.

nodes.label: Enrichment
nodes.detail: Add context, reputation, provenance, and confidence level to indicators.
nodes.exam: Stale threat intelligence generates false positives.

nodes.label: SIEM Correlation
nodes.detail: Apply correlation rules and produce an alert score.
nodes.exam: An overly broad rule generates noise and analyst fatigue.

nodes.label: Verdict
nodes.detail: Classify: confirmed incident, suspicious, or false positive, with justification.
nodes.exam: A verdict must be documented and reversible.

nodes.label: Action
nodes.detail: Proportionate response: isolation, blocking, credential rotation.
nodes.exam: Tailor the response to the confidence level.

quiz.question: Which system applies rules to turn IOCs into a scored alert?

diagrams.title: Upstream AI Threats: Attacking Before Use
diagrams.subtitle: Before deployment, the model can be poisoned, backdoored, or contaminated via its dependencies.

nodes.label: Data Poisoning
nodes.detail: Alter training data to persistently bias the model's behavior.
nodes.exam: Upstream = before or during training.

nodes.label: Backdoor
nodes.detail: Inject an unlikely trigger that activates a specific behavior.
nodes.exam: Hard to detect with standard tests.

nodes.label: Third-Party Models
nodes.detail: Compromised pre-trained models or libraries downloaded from a repository.
nodes.exam: Verify model provenance and checksums.

nodes.label: Labeling
nodes.detail: Falsify labels to corrupt supervised learning.
nodes.exam: Label quality is a security issue.

nodes.label: Training
nodes.detail: The pipeline aggregates data, code, hyperparameters, and libraries.
nodes.exam: Secure every stage of the ML pipeline.

nodes.label: Compromised Model
nodes.detail: The trained model produces biased or malicious responses once deployed.
nodes.exam: A poisoned model remains dangerous after deployment.

nodes.label: Validation
nodes.detail: Independent test sets, model checksums, and pipeline review.
nodes.exam: A single test set is not enough.

nodes.label: Monitoring
nodes.detail: Continuous monitoring for drift and unexpected behaviors.
nodes.exam: Drift can be natural or adversarial.

quiz.question: Which threat modifies training data to bias the model?

diagrams.title: Downstream AI Threats: From Prompt to Leak
diagrams.subtitle: After deployment, prompt injection, jailbreaking, and tool abuse threaten confidentiality and reliability.

nodes.label: Prompt Injection
nodes.detail: Malicious instructions hidden in input or an ingested document.
nodes.exam: The LLM does not always distinguish data from instructions.

nodes.label: Jailbreak
nodes.detail: Phrasing, roleplay, or encoding designed to bypass restrictions.
nodes.exam: Guardrails are not an absolute guarantee.

nodes.label: RAG Context
nodes.detail: Poisoning of retrieval sources or conversational memory.
nodes.exam: A contaminated source infects future responses.

nodes.label: Data Leak
nodes.detail: Disclosure of secrets, personal data, or confidential information.
nodes.exam: DLP also applies to LLM outputs.

nodes.label: Hallucination
nodes.detail: False yet convincing response, with fabricated citations.
nodes.exam: Always verify facts and sources.

nodes.label: Tool Abuse
nodes.detail: Unintended tool calls triggering sensitive actions.
nodes.exam: Apply least privilege to LLM tools.

nodes.label: Guardrails
nodes.detail: Input/output filters, sandboxing, and DLP controls around the model.
nodes.exam: Defense in depth: filter + sandbox + review.
